items.stem: Which economist, Nobel laureate in 1998, wrote Development as Freedom (1999)?
items.answer: Amartya Sen
items.markingKey: Amartya Sen. Sen’s capability approach underpins the Human Development Index and the MPI.

items.stem: Explain why poverty is a political as well as an economic issue.
items.answer: Who counts as poor, which measures are used and how resources are distributed are political choices; poverty is shaped by state policy, power and exclusion, and in turn affects legitimacy and stability.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Who counts as poor, which measures are used and how resources are distributed are political choices; poverty is shaped by state policy, power and exclusion, and in turn affects legitimacy and stability. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the intensity of poverty (A) and the incidence of poverty (H).
items.answer: Incidence is the proportion of people who are poor; intensity is the average share of weighted deprivations that poor people experience. The MPI is H × A.
items.markingKey: Incidence is the proportion of people who are poor; intensity is the average share of weighted deprivations that poor people experience. The MPI is H × A. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe COVID-19 and global poverty (2020) and explain what it reveals about the vulnerability of the near-poor.
items.answer: The World Bank estimated that the pandemic pushed around 70 million people into extreme poverty in 2020, the largest single-year increase since global monitoring began. Shocks push people just above the line back into poverty, showing that poverty is dynamic and depends on social protection.
items.markingKey: Context (The World Bank estimated that the pandemic pushed around 70 million people into extreme poverty in 2020, the largest single-year increase since global monitoring began.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Shocks push people just above the line back into poverty, showing that poverty is dynamic and depends on social protection. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the vulnerability of the near-poor.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Poverty is simply a lack of money." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sen and the MPI show poverty also involves deprivation of health, education, voice and security; people above an income line can still be multidimensionally poor.
items.markingKey: Sen and the MPI show poverty also involves deprivation of health, education, voice and security; people above an income line can still be multidimensionally poor. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Survey data for a district modelled on highland Peru show 540,000 multidimensionally poor people out of 1,500,000 residents. On average, poor people are deprived in 38% of weighted indicators. Calculate the headcount ratio (H) and the MPI (H × A) to three decimal places, and explain why two regions with the same H could have different MPI values. [4]
items.markingKey: M1 H = 540,000/1,500,000 = 0.36; M1 MPI = H × A; A1 MPI = 0.137. R1 regions with equal H can differ in A, the intensity of deprivation among the poor, so the MPI also reflects how poor the poor are.

items.stem:
Source D
Of the 1.1 billion people living in acute multidimensional poverty, half are children under 18. Around 83 per cent live in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, and the majority live in rural areas.
— UNDP and OPHI, Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (2023) (adapted)

Using evidence from Source D, explain how the source shows that poverty is unevenly distributed. [4]
items.answer: It shows concentration by age (children), region (Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia) and location (rural areas), implying that poverty reflects unequal access to services and power.
items.markingKey: It shows concentration by age (children), region (Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia) and location (rural areas), implying that poverty reflects unequal access to services and power. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Examine the view that poverty in the Global South is mainly caused by the structure of the global economy. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Global structures constrain poor states, but domestic governance and conflict explain much of the variation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: dependency theory; debt burdens and commodity dependence; unfair trade rules and subsidies in rich states. Arguments against: East Asian states escaped poverty within the global economy; governance and corruption matter; conflict is a major cause (fragile states). Possible judgement: Global structures constrain poor states, but domestic governance and conflict explain much of the variation. items.stem: Explain why income-based poverty lines have been criticised.
items.answer: A single dollar figure ignores differences in needs and prices, hides deprivations in health, education and housing, and depends on contested purchasing power adjustments; small changes to the line move hundreds of millions in or out of poverty.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A single dollar figure ignores differences in needs and prices, hides deprivations in health, education and housing, and depends on contested purchasing power adjustments; small changes to the line move hundreds of millions in or out of poverty. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why the MPI may give a different picture of poverty from income measures.
items.answer: It counts overlapping deprivations – such as lack of schooling, clean water or electricity – which can exist even when income is above the line, and it shows the intensity as well as the incidence of poverty.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It counts overlapping deprivations – such as lack of schooling, clean water or electricity – which can exist even when income is above the line, and it shows the intensity as well as the incidence of poverty. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.answer: Incidence is the proportion of people who are poor; intensity is the average share of weighted deprivations that poor people experience. The MPI is H × A.
items.markingKey: Incidence is the proportion of people who are poor; intensity is the average share of weighted deprivations that poor people experience. The MPI is H × A. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: In an MPI training exercise based on western Nepal, the Gurung household shows deprivations in years of schooling, assets, housing, electricity, drinking water. In the global MPI each health and education indicator carries a weight of 1/6 and each living-standards indicator 1/18. Calculate the household’s deprivation score and state how it is classified (poor ≥ 1/3; severe ≥ 1/2; vulnerable 1/5 to below 1/3). [3]
items.answer: Score = 7/18 ≈ 38.9% → multidimensionally poor
items.markingKey: M1 weights applied correctly (3/18 + 1/18 + 1/18 + 1/18 + 1/18); A1 score = 7/18 ≈ 38.9%; A1 classification: multidimensionally poor.

items.stem: "Multidimensional measures of poverty are more useful than income measures for policy-makers." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Multidimensional measures are better for designing policy, while income measures remain useful for tracking trends.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: identify which deprivation to target (India’s sanitation programmes); reflect capability approach; capture intensity. Arguments against: income lines are simple and comparable over time; MPI weights are arbitrary; data collected less frequently. Supported judgement: Multidimensional measures are better for designing policy, while income measures remain useful for tracking trends. items.stem: Which economist argued in Dead Aid (2009) that aid dependency harms African development?
items.answer: Dambisa Moyo
items.markingKey: C. Moyo argued that aid fuels corruption and discourages investment.

items.stem: Mateo writes: "Most rich countries give 0.7 per cent of their income in aid." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The OECD donors’ average is around 0.3–0.4 per cent; only a handful meet the target, and several large donors, including the UK and the USA, cut aid in 2025.
items.markingKey: The OECD donors’ average is around 0.3–0.4 per cent; only a handful meet the target, and several large donors, including the UK and the USA, cut aid in 2025. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why debt relief can help reduce poverty.
items.answer: Money no longer spent on debt service can be redirected to health and education; HIPC required governments to prepare poverty reduction strategies, and spending on social services rose in several recipients.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Money no longer spent on debt service can be redirected to health and education; HIPC required governments to prepare poverty reduction strategies, and spending on social services rose in several recipients. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Bolsa Família, Brazil and explain what it reveals about social protection as a response to poverty.
items.answer: Launched under President Lula in 2003, the programme made monthly payments to poor families on condition of school attendance and health checks; extreme poverty fell substantially during the 2000s. Targeted cash transfers combined immediate income support with investment in human capabilities, at a cost of about 0.5 per cent of GDP.
items.markingKey: Context (Launched under President Lula in 2003, the programme made monthly payments to poor families on condition of school attendance and health checks; extreme poverty fell substantially during the 2000s.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Targeted cash transfers combined immediate income support with investment in human capabilities, at a cost of about 0.5 per cent of GDP. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to social protection as a response to poverty.

items.stem:
Source C
Aid has been, and continues to be, an unmitigated political, economic and humanitarian disaster for most parts of the developing world. It has fostered dependency, encouraged corruption and allowed governments to avoid accountability to their own citizens.
— Dambisa Moyo, Dead Aid (2009) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source C, explain how the source reflects a critique of top-down approaches to poverty. [4]
items.answer: It argues that aid flowing from donors to governments weakens domestic accountability and markets, reflecting the view that externally designed, state-led interventions undermine development.
items.markingKey: It argues that aid flowing from donors to governments weakens domestic accountability and markets, reflecting the view that externally designed, state-led interventions undermine development. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Social protection is more effective than economic growth in reducing poverty."
items.answer: Growth and social protection are complementary; growth funds protection, and protection makes growth inclusive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cash transfers reach the poorest directly; growth is not always pro-poor; protection against shocks (COVID-19). Arguments against: China’s poverty reduction came mainly from growth; social protection needs revenues from growth; jobs are the main route out of poverty. Supported judgement: Growth and social protection are complementary; growth funds protection, and protection makes growth inclusive.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "microfinance".
items.answer: The provision of small loans, savings and insurance to poor people without access to conventional banking, pioneered by Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the provision of small loans, savings and insurance to poor people without access to conventional banking, pioneered by Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between bilateral aid and multilateral aid.
items.answer: Bilateral aid goes directly from one government to another and often reflects donor interests; multilateral aid is channelled through international organisations such as the World Bank or UN agencies, pooling resources and reducing political conditions.
items.markingKey: Bilateral aid goes directly from one government to another and often reflects donor interests; multilateral aid is channelled through international organisations such as the World Bank or UN agencies, pooling resources and reducing political conditions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source D
The end of extreme poverty is within reach. Targeted investments in health, education, clean water and agriculture, financed by rich countries meeting their aid promises, can enable the poorest to climb onto the first rung of the ladder of development.
— Jeffrey Sachs, The End of Poverty (2005) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source D about responses to poverty. [3]
items.answer: extreme poverty can be ended; targeted investments in health, education, water and agriculture are needed; rich countries should meet their aid promises
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: extreme poverty can be ended; targeted investments in health, education, water and agriculture are needed; rich countries should meet their aid promises. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: "Microfinance has lifted most borrowers out of poverty." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Evidence from randomised trials (e.g. Banerjee and Duflo) shows modest effects on business activity but no large average rise in income or consumption.
items.markingKey: Evidence from randomised trials (e.g. Banerjee and Duflo) shows modest effects on business activity but no large average rise in income or consumption. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Social protection is more effective than economic growth in reducing poverty." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Growth and social protection are complementary; growth funds protection, and protection makes growth inclusive.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: cash transfers reach the poorest directly; growth is not always pro-poor; protection against shocks (COVID-19). Arguments against: China’s poverty reduction came mainly from growth; social protection needs revenues from growth; jobs are the main route out of poverty. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Gini coefficient"?
options: A state with weak capacity or legitimacy to provide security and basic services, at high risk of conflict; by 2030 most of the world’s extreme poor are expected to live in fragile and conflict-affected settings
Ted Gurr’s concept of the gap between what people believe they are entitled to and what they actually have, which can generate frustration and political violence
A measure of income or wealth inequality ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything), sometimes expressed from 0 to 100
Paul Collier’s idea that poverty increases the risk of civil war, and war in turn deepens poverty, creating a self-reinforcing cycle
items.answer: A measure of income or wealth inequality ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything), sometimes expressed from 0 to 100
items.markingKey: C. "Gini coefficient" is a measure of income or wealth inequality ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything), sometimes expressed from 0 to 100.

items.stem: A student claims: "The poorest countries always have the most protests." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Mass protest is common in middle-income countries with high inequality and rising expectations, such as Chile (2019) or Tunisia (2010–11).
items.markingKey: Mass protest is common in middle-income countries with high inequality and rising expectations, such as Chile (2019) or Tunisia (2010–11). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why conflict tends to deepen poverty.
items.answer: War destroys infrastructure, displaces people, diverts spending to the military and deters investment; Collier estimated that a typical civil war reduces growth by around 2 percentage points a year.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: War destroys infrastructure, displaces people, diverts spending to the military and deters investment; Collier estimated that a typical civil war reduces growth by around 2 percentage points a year. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Source D
Rising inequality is fuelling discontent, eroding trust in institutions and contributing to political polarisation. Where people feel excluded from the benefits of growth, protest and support for anti-system movements increase.
— UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, World Social Report (2020) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source D, explain why the source suggests inequality is a threat to political stability. [3]
items.answer: Exclusion from the benefits of growth undermines the legitimacy of institutions, encouraging protest and support for anti-system movements, which can destabilise politics.
items.markingKey: Exclusion from the benefits of growth undermines the legitimacy of institutions, encouraging protest and support for anti-system movements, which can destabilise politics. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Côte d’Ivoire’s civil conflict (2002–2011) shows horizontal inequalities and conflict.
items.answer: Northern, largely Muslim groups faced economic disadvantage and exclusion from citizenship and political office, which contributed to civil war and post-election violence in 2010–11. Overlapping economic and political exclusion of a regional and religious group created mobilised grievances, as Stewart’s theory predicts.
items.markingKey: Context (Northern, largely Muslim groups faced economic disadvantage and exclusion from citizenship and political office, which contributed to civil war and post-election violence in 2010–11.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Overlapping economic and political exclusion of a regional and religious group created mobilised grievances, as Stewart’s theory predicts. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to horizontal inequalities and conflict.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Reducing poverty is the most effective way to prevent conflict."
items.answer: Poverty reduction helps prevent conflict when combined with inclusive politics and reduced group inequality.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: conflict trap; grievances over jobs and food; development as conflict prevention. Arguments against: inclusive governance matters more; growth can increase inequality and tension; greed and political exclusion also drive conflict. Supported judgement: Poverty reduction helps prevent conflict when combined with inclusive politics and reduced group inequality.

items.stem: Which economist argued that low income, slow growth and dependence on primary commodities raise the risk of civil war (the “conflict trap”)?
items.answer: Paul Collier
items.markingKey: A. Collier set out the argument in The Bottom Billion (2007).

items.stem: Explain the difference between grievance explanations and greed explanations of instability.
items.answer: Greed explanations focus on opportunities for rebels to profit (e.g. lootable resources); grievance explanations focus on perceived injustice such as poverty, inequality and exclusion.
items.markingKey: Greed explanations focus on opportunities for rebels to profit (e.g. lootable resources); grievance explanations focus on perceived injustice such as poverty, inequality and exclusion. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: fuels discontent; erodes trust in institutions; contributes to polarisation and support for anti-system movements
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: fuels discontent; erodes trust in institutions; contributes to polarisation and support for anti-system movements. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Arab Spring in Tunisia (2010–11) and explain what it reveals about relative deprivation and instability.
items.answer: Youth unemployment, regional inequality and corruption led to mass protests after Mohamed Bouazizi’s self-immolation; President Ben Ali fled in January 2011. Educated young people whose expectations exceeded their opportunities mobilised against a regime seen as corrupt, illustrating Gurr’s theory.
items.markingKey: Context (Youth unemployment, regional inequality and corruption led to mass protests after Mohamed Bouazizi’s self-immolation; President Ben Ali fled in January 2011.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Educated young people whose expectations exceeded their opportunities mobilised against a regime seen as corrupt, illustrating Gurr’s theory. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to relative deprivation and instability.

items.stem: What are the three dimensions of the global Multidimensional Poverty Index?
items.answer: Health, education and living standards
items.markingKey: D. The ten indicators are equally weighted across the three dimensions.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The provision of small loans, savings and insurance to poor people without access to conventional banking, pioneered by Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh"?
items.answer: microfinance
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of microfinance.

items.stem: The self-immolation of which street vendor in Tunisia in December 2010 helped trigger the Arab Spring?
items.answer: Mohamed Bouazizi
items.markingKey: Mohamed Bouazizi. His protest against police harassment symbolised economic exclusion and injustice.

items.stem: A student claims: "Global poverty has fallen evenly in all regions since 1990." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The fall was concentrated in East and South Asia; the number of extremely poor people in Sub-Saharan Africa has risen, and COVID-19 caused the first increase in global extreme poverty in a generation in 2020.
items.markingKey: The fall was concentrated in East and South Asia; the number of extremely poor people in Sub-Saharan Africa has risen, and COVID-19 caused the first increase in global extreme poverty in a generation in 2020. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between top-down approaches to poverty reduction and bottom-up approaches.
items.answer: Top-down approaches are designed by states or international institutions (structural adjustment, large infrastructure projects); bottom-up approaches start from communities and individuals (microfinance, participatory development).
items.markingKey: Top-down approaches are designed by states or international institutions (structural adjustment, large infrastructure projects); bottom-up approaches start from communities and individuals (microfinance, participatory development). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between horizontal inequality and vertical inequality.
items.answer: Vertical inequality is inequality between individuals or households across a whole population (measured by the Gini coefficient); horizontal inequality is inequality between culturally defined groups.
items.markingKey: Vertical inequality is inequality between individuals or households across a whole population (measured by the Gini coefficient); horizontal inequality is inequality between culturally defined groups. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the incidence of poverty (H) and the intensity of poverty (A).
items.answer: Incidence is the proportion of people who are poor; intensity is the average share of weighted deprivations that poor people experience. The MPI is H × A.
items.markingKey: Incidence is the proportion of people who are poor; intensity is the average share of weighted deprivations that poor people experience. The MPI is H × A. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why microfinance has been criticised.
items.answer: Randomised studies found modest effects on average incomes, high interest rates can trap borrowers in debt (as in Andhra Pradesh in 2010), and commercialisation shifted it away from poverty reduction.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Randomised studies found modest effects on average incomes, high interest rates can trap borrowers in debt (as in Andhra Pradesh in 2010), and commercialisation shifted it away from poverty reduction. items.answer: Mass protest is common in middle-income countries with high inequality and rising expectations, such as Chile (2019) or Tunisia (2010–11).

— Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (1999) (paraphrased)

items.answer: poverty is the deprivation of basic capabilities; it is not merely low income; what matters is what people are able to do and be
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: poverty is the deprivation of basic capabilities; it is not merely low income; what matters is what people are able to do and be. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Zambia’s debt default and restructuring (2020–2024) shows the politics of debt relief.
items.answer: Zambia became the first African state to default during the pandemic; restructuring under the G20 Common Framework took years, partly because of negotiations involving Chinese lenders and private bondholders. Debt relief depends on bargaining between creditors with different interests, showing how power shapes responses to poverty.
items.markingKey: Context (Zambia became the first African state to default during the pandemic; restructuring under the G20 Common Framework took years, partly because of negotiations involving Chinese lenders and private bondholders.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Debt relief depends on bargaining between creditors with different interests, showing how power shapes responses to poverty. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the politics of debt relief.

Group inequalities – in political power, economic resources and social status – are an important source of conflict. When cultural differences coincide with economic and political differences between groups, this can cause deep resentment that may lead to violent struggles.
— Frances Stewart, Horizontal Inequalities and Conflict (2008) (paraphrased)

Identify three types of group inequality mentioned in Source B. [3]
items.answer: political power; economic resources; social status
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: political power; economic resources; social status. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem: With reference to India’s fall in multidimensional poverty (2005/06–2019/21), explain how it illustrates multidimensional measurement of poverty.
items.answer: The UNDP and OPHI reported that about 415 million people in India left multidimensional poverty over 15 years, linked to expanded sanitation, cooking fuel, electricity and schooling programmes. Progress was driven by improvements in specific non-income indicators, showing how the MPI captures changes that income data alone would miss.
items.markingKey: Context (The UNDP and OPHI reported that about 415 million people in India left multidimensional poverty over 15 years, linked to expanded sanitation, cooking fuel, electricity and schooling programmes.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Examine the view that foreign aid does more harm than good in reducing poverty. Use relevant key concepts and named examples in your answer. [15]
items.answer: Aid is not inherently harmful; its effects depend on how it is targeted, governed and owned by recipients.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: dependency and corruption (Moyo); tied aid serves donors; aid can prolong authoritarian rule. Arguments against: health aid saved millions (Global Fund, Gavi); aid supports fragile states and emergencies; cuts in 2025 threatened programmes. Possible judgement: Aid is not inherently harmful; its effects depend on how it is targeted, governed and owned by recipients. items.stem: Discuss the relationship between poverty, inequality and political instability, with reference to two examples. [15]
items.answer: Poverty and inequality increase instability when combined with exclusion and unresponsive governance.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: relative deprivation; horizontal inequalities (Côte d’Ivoire); Arab Spring and Chile; Collier’s conflict trap. Possible judgement: Poverty and inequality increase instability when combined with exclusion and unresponsive governance. items.stem:
Source B
Poverty must be seen as the deprivation of basic capabilities rather than merely as lowness of incomes. Income is only instrumentally significant; what matters is what people are able to do and to be.
— Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (1999) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source B, explain how the source challenges income-based measures of poverty. [4]
items.answer: By arguing that income is only a means, the source suggests that measures like the $3.00 line miss deprivations in health, education and freedom, supporting multidimensional measures such as the MPI.
items.markingKey: By arguing that income is only a means, the source suggests that measures like the $3.00 line miss deprivations in health, education and freedom, supporting multidimensional measures such as the MPI. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: "Social protection is more effective than economic growth in reducing poverty." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Growth and social protection are complementary; growth funds protection, and protection makes growth inclusive.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cash transfers reach the poorest directly; growth is not always pro-poor; protection against shocks (COVID-19). Arguments against: China’s poverty reduction came mainly from growth; social protection needs revenues from growth; jobs are the main route out of poverty. Supported judgement: Growth and social protection are complementary; growth funds protection, and protection makes growth inclusive. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A condition in which people cannot meet basic needs for food, water, shelter, health and education; the World Bank’s international (extreme) poverty line is $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing power parity, replacing $2.15 at 2017 prices in 2025"?
items.answer: absolute poverty
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of absolute poverty.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "official development assistance (ODA)"?
options: Amartya Sen’s view that poverty is the deprivation of the capabilities – real freedoms – people need to live the lives they have reason to value, not merely low income
Government aid to developing countries that promotes economic development and welfare and is concessional; the UN target is 0.7 per cent of donor gross national income
Policies and programmes, such as pensions, cash transfers and public works, that reduce poverty and vulnerability by protecting people against shocks
Having an income or standard of living well below the norm of one’s own society, often defined as below 50 or 60 per cent of median household income
items.answer: Government aid to developing countries that promotes economic development and welfare and is concessional; the UN target is 0.7 per cent of donor gross national income
items.markingKey: B. "official development assistance (ODA)" is government aid to developing countries that promotes economic development and welfare and is concessional; the UN target is 0.7 per cent of donor gross national income.

items.stem: Define the term "horizontal inequality".
items.answer: Frances Stewart’s term for inequality between culturally defined groups (ethnic, religious, regional), which is more strongly associated with conflict than inequality between individuals
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: Frances Stewart’s term for inequality between culturally defined groups (ethnic, religious, regional), which is more strongly associated with conflict than inequality between individuals. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: "Poverty is simply a lack of money." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Sen and the MPI show poverty also involves deprivation of health, education, voice and security; people above an income line can still be multidimensionally poor.
items.markingKey: Sen and the MPI show poverty also involves deprivation of health, education, voice and security; people above an income line can still be multidimensionally poor. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the effectiveness of foreign aid is debated.
items.answer: Supporters (Sachs) argue aid funds health, education and infrastructure that markets will not provide; critics (Moyo, Easterly) argue it creates dependency, supports corrupt elites and serves donor interests.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Supporters (Sachs) argue aid funds health, education and infrastructure that markets will not provide; critics (Moyo, Easterly) argue it creates dependency, supports corrupt elites and serves donor interests. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Inequality and poverty are the same thing." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Poverty is about deprivation below a threshold; inequality is about distribution. A country can reduce poverty while inequality rises, as China did after 1980.
items.markingKey: Poverty is about deprivation below a threshold; inequality is about distribution. A country can reduce poverty while inequality rises, as China did after 1980. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Global poverty has fallen evenly in all regions since 1990." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The fall was concentrated in East and South Asia; the number of extremely poor people in Sub-Saharan Africa has risen, and COVID-19 caused the first increase in global extreme poverty in a generation in 2020.
items.markingKey: The fall was concentrated in East and South Asia; the number of extremely poor people in Sub-Saharan Africa has risen, and COVID-19 caused the first increase in global extreme poverty in a generation in 2020. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Microfinance has lifted most borrowers out of poverty." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Evidence from randomised trials (e.g. Banerjee and Duflo) shows modest effects on business activity but no large average rise in income or consumption.
items.markingKey: Evidence from randomised trials (e.g. Banerjee and Duflo) shows modest effects on business activity but no large average rise in income or consumption. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between vertical inequality and horizontal inequality.
items.answer: Vertical inequality is inequality between individuals or households across a whole population (measured by the Gini coefficient); horizontal inequality is inequality between culturally defined groups.
items.markingKey: Vertical inequality is inequality between individuals or households across a whole population (measured by the Gini coefficient); horizontal inequality is inequality between culturally defined groups. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

Outline three points made in Source A about the measurement and politics of poverty. [3]
items.answer: poverty is the deprivation of basic capabilities; it is not merely low income; what matters is what people are able to do and be

items.stem:
Source D
The end of extreme poverty is within reach. Targeted investments in health, education, clean water and agriculture, financed by rich countries meeting their aid promises, can enable the poorest to climb onto the first rung of the ladder of development.
— Jeffrey Sachs, The End of Poverty (2005) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source D, explain how the source supports a liberal approach to poverty reduction. [4]
items.answer: It argues that international cooperation and aid can remove “poverty traps”, allowing the poor to join markets and grow – a liberal, internationalist view of development.
items.markingKey: It argues that international cooperation and aid can remove “poverty traps”, allowing the poor to join markets and grow – a liberal, internationalist view of development. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Arab Spring in Tunisia (2010–11) shows relative deprivation and instability.
items.answer: Youth unemployment, regional inequality and corruption led to mass protests after Mohamed Bouazizi’s self-immolation; President Ben Ali fled in January 2011. Educated young people whose expectations exceeded their opportunities mobilised against a regime seen as corrupt, illustrating Gurr’s theory.
items.markingKey: Context (Youth unemployment, regional inequality and corruption led to mass protests after Mohamed Bouazizi’s self-immolation; President Ben Ali fled in January 2011.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Educated young people whose expectations exceeded their opportunities mobilised against a regime seen as corrupt, illustrating Gurr’s theory. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to relative deprivation and instability.

items.stem: A province in Sindh, Pakistan has a population of 1,500,000. Of these, 780,000 people are identified as multidimensionally poor, and the average deprivation score among the poor is 51%. Calculate the headcount ratio (H) and the MPI value (H × A), giving the MPI to three decimal places. [3]

Source B
Aid has been, and continues to be, an unmitigated political, economic and humanitarian disaster for most parts of the developing world. It has fostered dependency, encouraged corruption and allowed governments to avoid accountability to their own citizens.
— Dambisa Moyo, Dead Aid (2009) (paraphrased)

Outline three points made in Source B about responses to poverty. [3]
items.answer: it has fostered dependency; it has encouraged corruption; it allows governments to avoid accountability to citizens
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: it has fostered dependency; it has encouraged corruption; it allows governments to avoid accountability to citizens. Points must be drawn from the source; accept close paraphrase. Own knowledge is not credited.

items.stem:
Source B
Group inequalities – in political power, economic resources and social status – are an important source of conflict. When cultural differences coincide with economic and political differences between groups, this can cause deep resentment that may lead to violent struggles.
— Frances Stewart, Horizontal Inequalities and Conflict (2008) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source B, explain how the source helps to explain the link between inequality and conflict. [4]
items.answer: It argues that inequality between groups, rather than between individuals, creates collective resentment that can be mobilised, especially when cultural, economic and political differences coincide.
items.markingKey: It argues that inequality between groups, rather than between individuals, creates collective resentment that can be mobilised, especially when cultural, economic and political differences coincide. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: "Inequality is a greater threat to political stability than absolute poverty." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Inequality is more likely to trigger protest, but extreme poverty is more closely linked to civil war risk.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: relative deprivation (Gurr); Arab Spring and Chile in middle-income states; horizontal inequality and conflict. Arguments against: conflict trap is concentrated in the poorest states (Collier); fragile states are mostly very poor; poverty limits state capacity. Supported judgement: Inequality is more likely to trigger protest, but extreme poverty is more closely linked to civil war risk. items.stem: "Poverty in the Global South is mainly caused by the structure of the global economy." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Global structures constrain poor states, but domestic governance and conflict explain much of the variation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: dependency theory; debt burdens and commodity dependence; unfair trade rules and subsidies in rich states. Arguments against: East Asian states escaped poverty within the global economy; governance and corruption matter; conflict is a major cause (fragile states). items.stem: Evaluate the effectiveness of debt relief as a response to poverty. [15]
items.answer: Debt relief has freed resources for social spending, but without fairer lending it offers only temporary relief.
